lead: A wide adder is slow because the carry must reach the last bit. Three architectures attack that chain without changing the final arithmetic. Carry select computes each block twice, with carry in 0 and 1, then selects. Carry skip passes the carry over a block whose bits all propagate. Carry save never propagates the carry inside a row: it keeps a sum vector and a carry vector for a later adder. The names CSL, CSK and CSA appear in datapath and multiplier design.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the full adder and for generate g and propagate p.

blocks.text: Carry select splits an n-bit adder into blocks of k bits. Each block contains two ripple adders. One assumes its carry in is 0. The other assumes 1. Both run at the same time.

For each sum bit in the block, a multiplexer picks the output of the correct adder. The select signal is the real carry coming from the lower block. The carry out of the block is also selected. No sum bit waits for the lower block; only the final selection waits.

Take a = 1011 (11) and b = 0110 (6), split into two-bit blocks. Low block (bits 1:0) adds 11 and 10 with carry in 0: sum 01, carry out 1. High block (bits 3:2) adds 10 and 01. With carry in 0 it gives sum 11, carry out 0. With carry in 1 it gives sum 00, carry out 1. The real carry is 1, so the multiplexers select the carry-in-1 result. The sum is 1 00 01 = 10001 (17).

Area is the cost. A plain two-bit block needs two full adders. A carry-select block needs four full adders plus three 2:1 multiplexers: two for the sum bits and one for the carry out. A square-root layout duplicates only high blocks in a tree. The first block is a single ripple adder. Later blocks get more copies with fixed carry assumptions. Delay falls to about one block ripple plus a multiplexer tree, while area stays proportional to n — roughly double that of a plain ripple adder when each block holds two copies. The name square-root adder comes from the √n choice of block size; carry select and carry skip are different architectures that both end up with square-root-style delay.

sections.h3: Carry skip: bypass a propagating block

blocks.text: Carry skip, also called carry bypass, uses the propagate signal p_i = a_i XOR b_i from Chapter 4.1. A bit propagates a carry when p_i = 1: a carry in produces a carry out. For a block from bit m to bit n, define block propagate P = p_m · p_{m+1} · ... · p_n. The dot means AND.

If P = 1, every bit in the block propagates. Any carry entering the block will leave it unchanged. A multiplexer then sends the incoming carry straight to the next block, bypassing the ripple chain. If P = 0, at least one bit stops or generates a carry, so the block uses its normal ripple carry out.

The block size k controls delay. Small blocks skip often but add many multiplexers. Large blocks ripple too far inside each block. A common estimate is T_skip ≈ (k + n/k) t_gate, where n is the adder width in bits, k is block width in bits, and t_gate is one gate delay. This is smallest near k = √n. The name square-root adder comes from this √n choice of block size; carry skip and carry select are different architectures, and both can have square-root-style delay. For a 32-bit adder the useful block size is near 5 or 6 bits. The carry skip adder is cheap: one AND chain and one multiplexer per block.

sections.h3: Carry save: keep the carry for later

blocks.text: A carry save adder does not try to finish the sum. It takes three numbers and reduces them to two. Each column uses one full adder as a 3:2 compressor. The full adder adds three input bits at the same position and produces a sum bit s_i and a carry bit c_i. The carry bit belongs one place to the left.

For inputs a, b and d, the row produces S = s_{n-1}...s_0 and raw carry bits c_{n-1}...c_0. The arithmetic identity is a + b + d = S + 2C, where C is the raw carry word c_{n-1}...c_0. In hardware the shifted carry vector is C' = 2C, so a + b + d = S + C'. A final carry propagate adder, such as the ripple or look-ahead adder of Chapter 4.1, adds S and C'. That final adder is the only place where a carry ripples.

The delay of the compressor row is one full adder delay. There is no carry chain across columns. The price is the final adder. In a multiplier, many partial-product rows are reduced by a tree of these 3:2 compressors. Wallace and Booth multipliers use exactly this block; see Chapter 4.4. The same row appears in a carry save adder used for multioperand addition.

blocks.text: Carry skip is the smallest change to a ripple adder. Carry select trades area for a shorter carry chain. Carry save is not a complete adder; it is a reduction step inside a larger datapath. A question that gives three numbers and asks for S and C is a carry save question. A question that gives carry-in 0 and carry-in 1 blocks is carry select. A question with p_i and a bypass multiplexer is carry skip.

figure.caption: Two ripple adders compute a block with carry in 0 and 1; the real lower-block carry selects the correct sum. For a = 1011 and b = 0110 the selected high sum is 00 and the final carry makes 10001 (17).

spec.title: Carry select adder
spec.aria: Two ripple adders run in parallel with different carry inputs and a multiplexer keeps the correct result.

examples.question: Use one row of carry save adders to add a = 1011 (11), b = 0110 (6) and d = 0101 (5). Give the sum vector S, the shifted carry vector C, and the final sum after the carry propagate adder.
steps: Column 0: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, so s0 = 0 and raw carry c0 = 1.
Column 1: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, so s1 = 0 and raw carry c1 = 1.
Column 2: 0 + 1 + 1 = 2, so s2 = 0 and raw carry c2 = 1.
Column 3: 1 + 0 + 0 = 1, so s3 = 1 and raw carry c3 = 0.
Sum vector S = s3 s2 s1 s0 = 1000 binary = 8.
Raw carry word = c3 c2 c1 c0 = 0111 binary = 7.
Shift the carry word left by one bit: C = 1110 binary = 14.
Final carry propagate add: S + C = 8 + 14 = 22. Check: 11 + 6 + 5 = 22.
examples.answer: S = 1000 (8), shifted carry C = 1110 (14), and the final sum is 10110 binary (22), which equals 11 + 6 + 5.
examples.check:
a = 0b1011
b = 0b0110
d = 0b0101
S = 0
C = 0
for i in range(4):
    total = ((a >> i) & 1) + ((b >> i) & 1) + ((d >> i) & 1)
    s = total & 1
    carry = total >> 1
    S |= s << i
    C |= carry << i
print(S)
print(C << 1)
print(S + (C << 1))

traps: Forgetting to shift the carry vector left by one bit before the final add. The raw carry word 0111 is 7, but the shifted vector 1110 is 14.
Expecting a carry save adder to produce a finished sum on its own. It only reduces three inputs to two vectors; a final carry propagate adder is still needed.
Using OR instead of AND for block propagate P in a carry skip adder. A carry crosses the whole block only when every p_i is 1.
In carry select, the multiplexer select is the real carry from the lower block, not the block's own carry out. Both candidate carries are already computed.

quiz.a: CSL is carry select, CSK is carry skip (carry bypass), and CSA is carry save adder.

quiz.q: Why does a carry save adder not give a finished sum?
quiz.a: It produces a sum vector S and a carry vector C without propagating carries across columns. The final value is S + 2C, so a carry propagate adder must add S and the shifted carry vector.

quiz.q: A carry save row gives S = 00101100 (44) and shifted carry C = 00011010 (26). What is the final sum?
For a 32-bit carry skip adder, compare k = 5 and k = 8 using T_skip ≈ (k + 32/k) t_gate. Which block size gives smaller delay?
quiz.a: k = 5 gives (5 + 6.4) = 11.4 t_gate. k = 8 gives (8 + 4) = 12 t_gate. k = 5 is smaller by 0.6 t_gate.

quiz.q: Carry select uses two ripple adders per block, yet it is faster. Explain why.
quiz.a: Both adders compute in parallel before the lower-block carry is ready. When the real carry arrives, a multiplexer selects one of two ready results. The delay becomes one block ripple plus multiplexer delay, not a carry chain through all n bits. The cost is extra area.

quiz.q: Why is P = p_m · p_{m+1} · ... · p_n written with AND, not OR?
quiz.a: A carry passes the block only if every bit propagates it. One p_i = 0 means that bit can stop or generate the carry, so the whole block cannot bypass.

quiz.q: What is a 3:2 compressor in a carry save adder?
quiz.a: A full adder used on one column. It compresses three input bits into one sum bit and one carry bit, with no carry chain across columns.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, carry-save rows sit inside multiplier trees and dot-product units, where many partial products must be reduced before one final adder. Carry-select ideas reappear in wide adders with redundant carry assumptions, and carry-skip logic appears in low-power adders where area matters more than the last few gates of delay. Modern synthesis tools choose among these structures automatically. Search for 'prefix adder', '3:2 compressor', 'redundant number system', and 'carry-save multiplier' to go further.
